classification.difficultyReason: Recognise ln(x) and its reciprocal as expressions in one unknown, clear the denominator subject to the original domain, solve the quadratic and convert both roots back to values of x.

answer.worked:
The original equation requires $x>3$. The power law gives
$$\begin{align*}\log_3\bigl((x-3)^2\bigr)&=\log_3(49)\\(x-3)^2&=49.\end{align*}$$
Since $x-3>0$, take the positive square root.
$$\begin{align*}x-3&=7\\x&=10.\end{align*}$$

The original equation requires $x>3$. Apply the power law and equate arguments.
$$\begin{align*}\log_5(x+3)&=\log_5\bigl((x-3)^2\bigr)\\x+3&=(x-3)^2\\x+3&=x^2-6x+9\\0&=x^2-7x+6\\0&=(x-1)(x-6).\end{align*}$$
The candidates are $x=1$ and $x=6$. Only $x=6$ satisfies $x>3$.

The original equation requires $x>\frac12$. Apply the product law and convert to index form.
$$\begin{align*}\log_3\bigl((2x-1)(2x+1)\bigr)&=1\\(2x-1)(2x+1)&=3\\4x^2-1&=3\\x^2&=1.\end{align*}$$
Of the candidates $x=-1$ and $x=1$, only $x=1$ satisfies $x>\frac12$.

answer.short:
$x=e^3$ or $x=e^4$.

Let $u=\ln(x)$ and solve the resulting quadratic.
answer.worked:
The original equation requires $x>0$ and $x\ne1$. Let $u=\ln(x)$, so $u\ne0$. Multiply by $u$ and factorise.
$$\begin{align*}u+\frac{12}{u}&=7\\u^2+12&=7u\\u^2-7u+12&=0\\(u-3)(u-4)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\ln(x)=3$ or $\ln(x)=4$, so $x=e^3$ or $x=e^4$. Both values satisfy the domain.
